With or without food (immediate-release); take ER with food
Avoid unless no alternative - possible fetal risk
Excreted in milk; use with caution
QT/ECG in at-risk patients, liver function, drug interactions
summary: Clarithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic for respiratory tract infections, skin infections, H. pylori eradication, and mycobacterial infections. It is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor with many significant drug interactions and can prolong the QT interval, so it must be avoided with several co-medications and in patients at arrhythmia risk.
indications: Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
Uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections

dosage.n: For 7 to 14 days depending on infection

dosage.d: 500 mg every 8 or 12 hours with a PPI +/- amoxicillin

dosage.n: For 10 days; max per adult dose

dosage.d: 7.5 mg/kg up to 500 mg every 12 hours
Reduce dose by 50% or double the dosing interval if CrCl <30 mL/min

admin: Immediate-release tablets: with or without food
Extended-release tablets: take with food and swallow whole
moa: Binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible bacteria, inhibiting protein synthesis (translocation step). Generally bacteriostatic; bactericidal at higher concentrations against some organisms. The 14-OH metabolite adds activity against H. influenzae.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to clarithromycin or other macrolides
Concomitant use with pimozide, cisapride, ergot alkaloids, lovastatin, simvastatin, lomitapide, or astemizole/terfenadine
History of cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction with prior clarithromycin
Concomitant colchicine in renal or hepatic impairment
relative: Coronary artery disease (increased long-term cardiac mortality signal)

preg: Avoid unless there is no suitable alternative. Animal studies showed adverse effects and human data are limited; some observational data suggest possible risk. Former US category C.
lact: Excreted into breast milk; use with caution. Monitor the infant for GI disturbance and candidiasis.
renal: In severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min), reduce the dose by half or double the dosing interval. Additional reduction is required when given with atazanavir or ritonavir.
hepatic: Use with caution; hepatic dysfunction (including cholestatic hepatitis) can occur. Discontinue immediately if signs of hepatitis develop.

major: Pimozide, cisapride, ergot alkaloids, lovastatin/simvastatin, lomitapide, astemizole/terfenadine (contraindicated)
QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics)
moderate: CYP3A4 substrates (calcium channel blockers, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, sildenafil)
interactions.food: Food does not significantly affect immediate-release; extended-release should be taken with food
interactions.diagnostics: May raise liver enzymes; monitor INR with warfarin

monitoring: ECG/QT in patients with risk factors
Liver function tests if prolonged or symptoms
counsel: Complete the full course even if you feel better
Report severe or persistent diarrhea (could be C. difficile)
Tell your prescriber all medicines you take - clarithromycin has many interactions
Report palpitations, fainting, yellowing of skin/eyes, or rash
A metallic/bitter taste is common and usually harmless
pk: Antibacterial effect within hours of absorption
Store at 20-25 C; do not refrigerate the reconstituted suspension
pearls: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor - always screen co-medications, especially statins and colchicine
Avoid in patients with QT prolongation or on other QT-prolonging drugs
Observational data link macrolides (incl. clarithromycin) to increased cardiovascular events in CAD
Better acid stability and tissue penetration than erythromycin with fewer GI effects
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up. Keep doses evenly spaced and finish the course.
overdose: Overdose mainly causes GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea) and possible QT effects. Management is supportive with removal of unabsorbed drug; clarithromycin is not appreciably removed by hemodialysis. No specific antidote.
